claims.text: Maternal history and culture results are unavailable, and the latest examination is missing, creating uncertainty about the presence of risk factors for early‑onset neonatal infection.
An immediate clinical assessment and physical examination of the baby, including vital signs, should be performed to identify any clinical indicators of possible early‑onset neonatal infection.
Given the gestational age of 28 weeks and age of 24 hours, close monitoring of vital signs, temperature, and feeding tolerance is warranted while awaiting further information.
If any clinical indicators of infection emerge during monitoring, escalation to full sepsis work‑up and empiric antibiotic therapy should be considered.
Parents should be informed that the lack of maternal data and incomplete examination introduces uncertainty, and that additional investigations will be undertaken to clarify the infant’s risk.
Repeat assessment and laboratory investigations (e.g., CRP, blood culture) should be scheduled once maternal information becomes available to guide ongoing management.

C3: Claim references gestational age 28 weeks and monitoring of vital signs, but evidence E1 does not specify gestational age or monitoring details beyond performing an assessment and physical exam.
C5: Claim advises informing parents about uncertainty and further investigations; evidence E1 does not provide guidance on parent communication.

C6: Claim recommends repeat assessment and lab investigations once maternal information is available; evidence E1 does not mention repeat assessment or specific labs to be scheduled after maternal data is obtained.

packet.evaluation_question: Maternal history and culture results are unavailable and the latest examination is missing. Explain uncertainty and the assessment needed without assuming normal findings. Gestation 28 weeks; age 24 hours; setting neonatal unit.

evidence.text: If there are any risk factors for early-onset neonatal infection (see box 1 on risk- factors for early-onset neonatal infection), or if there are clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection (see box 2 on clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection): • perform an immediate clinical assessment • review the maternal and neonatal history • carry out a physical examination of the baby, including an assessment of vital signs. [2021]

The Kaiser Permanente neonatal sepsis calculator can be used as an alternative to the framework outlined in recommendation 1.10.3 for babies born after 34+0 weeks of pregnancy who are being cared for in a neonatal unit, transitional care or postnatal ward. It should only be used if it is part of a prospective audit, which should record: • total number of babies assessed using the calculator • number of babies correctly identified by the calculator who develop a culture-confirmed neonatal infection • number of babies incorrectly identified by the calculator who do not develop a culture-confirmed neonatal infection • number of babies missed by the calculator who develop a culture-confirmed neonatal infection. [2021]

Offer an immediate birth (by induction of labour or caesarean birth) to women, trans men and non-binary people who are between 34 and 37 weeks' gestation who: • have prolonged prelabour rupture of membranes and • have group B streptococcal colonisation, bacteriuria or infection at any time in their current pregnancy. [2021]

Offer antibiotics during labour to women, trans men and non-binary people who: • are in pre-term labour or • have group B streptococcal colonisation, bacteriuria or infection during the current pregnancy or • have had group B streptococcal colonisation, bacteriuria or infection in a previous pregnancy, and have not had a negative test for group B streptococcus by enrichment culture or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on a rectovaginal swab samples collected between 35 and 37 weeks' gestation or 3 to 5 weeks before the anticipated delivery date in the current pregnancy or • have had a previous baby with an invasive group B streptococcal infection or • have a clinical diagnosis of chorioamnionitis. [2021]
